title: LATEST NEWS FOR IMMIGRANTS
description: USCIS has announced a rare and critical filing window for Green Card applications in **January 2026**. This window, opening **January 1 and closing January 31, 2026**, follows a significant advancement in the January 2026 Visa Bulletin, particularly for Indian professionals in the EB-1 and EB-5 categories. Key Details of the January Filing Window * **Window Duration:** Applications must be submitted between **January 1 and January 31, 2026**. * **Priority Categories:** The most significant gains are in the **EB-1** (priority workers) and **EB-5** (investor visa) categories for Indian applicants. * **Filing Flexibility:** USCIS has confirmed that applicants can use the **Dates for Filing** chart, which often allows for earlier submissions than the Final Action Dates chart. * **Mandatory Requirements:** Applicants must file their **medical examinations concurrently** with their Form I-485, as USCIS now requires these to be submitted at the same time for adjustment of status. Strategic Advice for Applicants Experts advise those eligible to act immediately, as such large advancements are historically often followed by **retrogression** (backwards movement of dates) later in the year. 1. **Assess Eligibility:** Check the [January 2026 Visa Bulletin](https://www.google.com/url?sa=i&source=web&rct=j&url=https://travel.state.gov/content/travel/en/legal/visa-law0/visa-bulletin.html&ved=2ahUKEwiw5e6IitaRAxWeLtAFHTLRB3UQy_kOegQIBxAB&opi=89978449&cd&psig=AOvVaw1innsHppNlA7S0QkyGrvar&ust=1766660691399000) once fully released to confirm your priority date is current. 2. **Gather Documentation:** Ensure all professional records and achievements, specifically for EB-1A cases, are thoroughly documented. 3. **Monitor Official Sites:** Regularly check the [USCIS Adjustment of Status Filing Charts](https://www.google.com/url?sa=i&source=web&rct=j&url=https://www.uscis.gov/green-card/green-card-processes-and-procedures/visa-availability-priority-dates/adjustment-of-status-filing-charts-from-the-visa-bulletin&ved=2ahUKEwiw5e6IitaRAxWeLtAFHTLRB3UQy_kOegQIBxAE&opi=89978449&cd&psig=AOvVaw1innsHppNlA7S0QkyGrvar&ust=1766660691399000) to verify which chart (Final Action vs. Dates for Filing) is authorized for use each month. from Google

title: Judge voids decision to end legal status of 60,000 immigrants from Honduras, Nepal and Nicaragua
description: By [Camilo Montoya-Galvez](https://www.cbsnews.com/team/camilo-montoya-galvez/?ftag=CNM-00-10aab4i) Updated on: January 1, 2026 / 10:22 AM EST / CBS News A federal judge in California on Wednesday voided the Trump administration's move to terminate the [Temporary Protected Status](https://www.cbsnews.com/tag/temporary-protection-status/?ftag=CNM-00-10aab4i) of roughly 60,000 immigrants from Honduras, Nepal and Nicaragua, calling it a "pre-ordained decision." Homeland Security Secretary [Kristi Noem](https://www.cbsnews.com/tag/kristi-noem/?ftag=CNM-00-10aab4i) announced the termination of the TPS programs for Honduras, Nepal and Nicaragua in June and July, saying the three countries had recovered from the environmental disasters that prompted the U.S. government to grant their nationals temporary legal refuge. Created by Congress in 1990, the TPS policy allows the U.S. government to give certain foreigners deportation protections and work permits, temporarily, if their native countries are facing armed conflict, an environmental disaster or another emergency that makes their return unsafe. In late July, U.S. District Court Judge Trina Thompson [delayed](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/judge-delays-termination-of-legal-status-for-immigrants-from-honduras-nepal-and-nicaragua/?ftag=CNM-00-10aab4i) the termination of the TPS programs for Honduras, Nepal and Nicaragua, issuing a preliminary finding that the Trump administration failed to consider lingering problems in three nations and that the decision to terminate the policies was motivated by racial animus, or racial hostility. That ruling was paused in August by an appeals court, allowing the Trump administration to end the programs. But Thompson issued [a summary judgment](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.cand.452397/gov.uscourts.cand.452397.197.0.pdf) on Wednesday, finding that the effort to revoke the legal status of tens of thousands of Hondurans, Nepalis and Nicaraguans was unlawful. She said Noem's move "was preordained and pretextual rather than based on an objective review of the country conditions as required by the TPS statute and the (Administrative Procedures Act)." "The record specifically reflects that, before taking office, the Secretary made a pre-ordained decision to end TPS and influenced the conditions review process to facilitate TPS terminations for Honduras, Nicaragua, and Nepal," Thompson wrote in her order. The TPS designations for Honduras and Nicaragua were first created in the late 1990s, after the devastation caused by Hurricane Mitch, which killed thousands in Central America. Many of those previously enrolled in those programs arrived in the U.S. more than two decades ago. The TPS policy for Nepal was established in 2015, following a deadly earthquake in the small Asian nation. The Trump administration has mounted an aggressive effort to dismantle most TPS programs, arguing the policy attracts illegal immigration and that it has been abused by Democratic administrations and extended for far too long. It has also moved to terminate TPS protections for hundreds of thousands of immigrants from [Afghanistan](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/afghans-deportation-protections-ending/?ftag=CNM-00-10aab4i), Cameroon, Ethiopia, [Haiti](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/legal-status-haitian-migrants-expire-early-february/?ftag=CNM-00-10aab4i), Myanmar, [Sudan](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/temporary-protected-status-south-sudan-terminated/?ftag=CNM-00-10aab4i), Syria and [Venezuela](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/supreme-court-trump-temporary-protected-status-venezuelans/?ftag=CNM-00-10aab4i). In a statement, Assistant DHS Secretary Tricia McLaughlin called the judge's ruling "another lawless and activist order from the federal judiciary who continues to usurp the President's constitutional authority." "Under the previous administration Temporary Protected Status was abused to allow violent terrorists, criminals, and national security threats into our nation," McLaughlin said. "TPS was never designed to be permanent, yet previous administrations have used it as a de facto amnesty program for decades. Given the improved situation in each of these countries, now is the right time to conclude what was always intended to be a temporary designation." Ahilan Arulanantham, co-director of the UCLA Center for Immigration Law and Policy, said Wednesday's ruling should allow TPS holders from Honduras, Nicaragua and Nepal to work in the U.S. legally and prevent federal immigration officials from detaining and deporting them. "The court's decision today restores TPS protections for thousands of long-term law-abiding TPS-holding residents from Honduras, Nepal, and Nicaragua," Arulanantham said. ### More from CBS News [![ICE can access some Medicaid information for deportation efforts, judge says ](https://assets1-cbsnewsstatic-com.cdn.ampproject.org/ii/AW/s/assets1.cbsnewsstatic.com/hub/i/r/2025/11/20/571ca597-0d45-49fc-9290-d45b12d3d6a1/thumbnail/96x96/bb77b60b390a5a91a95a44b7927e01b9/gettyimages-2216629435.jpg# "ICE can access some Medicaid information for deportation efforts, judge says ")](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/ice-deportation-medicaid-information-judge-order/?intcid=CNR-02-0623&ftag=CNM-00-10aab4i) [ICE can access some Medicaid information for deportation efforts, judge says](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/ice-deportation-medicaid-information-judge-order/?intcid=CNR-02-0623&ftag=CNM-00-10aab4i) [![Mayor Johnson, Cmdr. title: Immigration attracts problem-solvers (and that’s a good thing)
description: One thing I’ve noticed over time is that immigration naturally attracts a very specific kind of person. Not better or worse — just different. People who move countries are usually willing to take risks, start over without guarantees, and figure things out as they go. You don’t leave behind familiarity, language, systems, and support unless you’re comfortable facing uncertainty and solving problems in real time. Immigration forces you to adapt constantly. When something doesn’t work, you can’t just complain — you have to find another path. New rules, new systems, new social codes, new ways of working. That process builds resilience, creativity, and a strong bias toward action. Over time, this mindset doesn’t just help immigrants integrate — it adds value to the places they move to. Immigrants often become builders, connectors, and contributors precisely because they’ve learned how to navigate complexity and create solutions from scratch. Platforms like this matter because they reduce unnecessary friction and let people focus on what they already do well: learning fast, adapting, and contributing. I’m glad spaces like this exist to support that journey.💪

title: U.K New Visa Rule
description: # U.K.’s New Visa Rule Starts Tomorrow, Affecting Connecting U.S. Passengers By[Emese Maczko](https://www.forbes.com/sites/emesemaczko/ "https://www.forbes.com/sites/emesemaczko/"), Contributor. Emese Maczko is a travel writer covering sustainable travel. Follow Author Jan 07, 2026, 08:15am ESTJan 08, 2026, 08:59am EST 0 ![Big Ben with bridge over Thames and flag of England against blue sky in London, England, UK](https://imageio.forbes.com/specials-images/imageserve/695e48f2e47620777fb31b01/Big-Ben-with-bridge-over-Thames-and-flag-of-England-against-blue-sky-in-London-/0x0.jpg?format=jpg&width=480 "Big Ben with bridge over Thames and flag of England against blue sky in London, England, UK") Big Ben with bridge over Thames and flag of England against blue sky in London, England, UK getty U.S. citizens traveling to the United Kingdom will face a new entry requirement starting January 8, 2025. This change applies not only to tourists and business travelers, but also to passengers transiting through U.K. airports. ## What Is The UK ETA? The [Electronic Travel Authorization](https://www.gov.uk/eta) functions as a digital pre-clearance system, similar to the U.S. ESTA program used for visa-waiver travelers entering the United States. U.S. passport holders must obtain an ETA before traveling to any part of the U.K., including England, Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland and the U.K.’s British Overseas Territories. The ETA, once approved, is valid for two years (or until the traveler’s passport expires, whichever comes first) and for multiple trips. It costs £16 (about $22) for each passenger, adults and children alike. ## Who Needs An ETA And Who Doesn’t U.S. citizens must apply for an ETA if they are traveling to or transiting through the U.K. and do not already hold a U.K. visa, a British or Irish passport or legal residency in the U.K. or the Republic of Ireland. Travelers who already [require a visa to enter the U.K.](https://www.gov.uk/check-uk-visa) under existing rules will continue to need a visa and should not apply for an ETA. The rules clearly state that travelers do not need an ETA if they are [transiting through a U.K. airport](https://www.gov.uk/uk-border-control/layovers-and-transiting) and will not pass through border control. However, if they pass through border control, they need the ETA. ![symbol](https://img.elements.video/pid-44f947fb-a5ce-41f1-a4fc-78dcf31c262a/44f947fb-a5ce-41f1-a4fc-78dcf31c262a/s1.png?width=72&height=72&fit=bounds "symbol") 00:00 03:12 Read More ![the UK Borders in Terminal 5 with arriving internation travel passengers waiting for immigration control and passport check.](https://imageio.forbes.com/specials-images/imageserve/695e4917903739f89257c5e7/the-UK-Borders--in-Terminal-5-with-arriving-internation-travel-passengers-waiting-for/0x0.jpg?height=484&width=480&fit=bounds "the UK Borders in Terminal 5 with arriving internation travel passengers waiting for immigration control and passport check.") UK Border in Terminal 5 of Heathrow in London with international passengers waiting for immigration control and passport check. getty ## Why This Matters For U.S. Travelers The new requirement ends decades of visa-free spontaneity for Americans flying to or through the U.K. Travelers who show up at the airport without an approved ETA risk being denied boarding, even if they are only connecting through a U.K. hub. The U.K. government allows a "[grace period](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/no-permission-no-travel-uk-set-to-enforce-eta-scheme)" until February 25, 2026, but travelers with upcoming trips or last-minute bookings are advised to apply as soon as possible. After February 25, 2026, airlines and other carriers will verify that travelers have an approved ETA before departure. This means passengers without an ETA will be denied boarding. ## How To Apply Applications must be submitted online through the [U.K. government’s official website](https://www.gov.uk/eta/apply) or via the U.K. ETA app, available on Google Play and the App Store. Forbes is protected by reCAPTCHA, and the Google [Privacy Policy](https://policies.google.com/privacy) and [Terms of Service](https://policies.google.com/terms) apply. [In an official statement](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/no-permission-no-travel-uk-set-to-enforce-eta-scheme), the U.K. government notes that most people currently receive a decision automatically within minutes. However, they still recommended allowing three working days to be on the safe side. ## More Countries Follow Suit Australia’s and New Zealand's long-running ETA for U.S. citizens has been in place for years. Brazil recently reinstated the electronic visa requirement for citizens of the United States (and Australia and Canada), effective April 10, 2025, while South Korea, on the contrary, [waived its K-ETA requirement for U.S. citizens](https://www.k-eta.go.kr/portal/board/viewboarddetail.do?bbsSn=299707) until December 31, 2026. The European Union is also working on its own system, the ETIAS (European Travel Information and Authorisation System), which is expected to launch in late 2026. Therefore, the U.K.’s ETA only marks another step in a global shift toward pre-screened international travel. But will these systems measurably speed up arrivals and improve security without creating new friction? Travelers clearly need to adopt a new habit in 2026 to check and apply for pre-authorization before their trips. The suspension will take effect on January 21 and will affect applicants from Latin America and the Caribbean, the Balkans, and several countries in South Asia, Africa, and the Middle East. ## Recommended Stories list of 1 item * list 1 of 1[Trump administration to suspend immigrant visa processing for 75 countries](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/1/14/trump-administration-to-suspend-immigrant-visa-processing-for-75-countries) end of list The change only affects people who want to move to the US permanently. It does not apply to visitors or short-term visa holders. But the latest move comes five months before the US hosts the FIFA World Cup along with Canada and Mexico, at a time when a series of crackdowns on immigrants, refugees, foreign students and visa applicants have raised questions about its attitude towards visitors. Here is what we know about the latest crackdown: ## What has the US administration announced? The State Department said it had told US consulates to stop processing immigrant visa applications from the affected countries. The move follows [a broader order issued](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2025/11/28/trump-pauses-immigration-from-third-world-countries-what-that-means) in November that tightened checks on potential immigrants who could become a financial burden on the US. “The Trump administration is bringing an end to the abuse of America’s immigration system by those who would extract wealth from the American people,” the department said in a statement. “Immigrant visa processing from these 75 countries will be paused while the State Department reassess immigration processing procedures to prevent the entry of foreign nationals who would take welfare and public benefits.” > > > ## How does it work? According to the State Department, nationals of the affected countries may still submit immigrant visa applications, but no immigrant visas will be approved or issued while the pause is in place. The US government has not indicated any deadline for when the suspension might be lifted. Advertisement An exception applies to dual nationals who apply using a valid passport from a country not included in the suspension. The suspension will not apply to non-immigrant, temporary, tourist, or business visas. ## Which countries are affected? The list of 75 countries includes: ## What other steps has Trump taken to restrict immigration? In recent months, the Trump administration has tightened immigration rules, particularly for people from countries whose vetting processes it has said are not robust enough, or that it believes are potential national security risks. The State Department has expanded limits on migration from these nations. In a statement released in January 2025, the White House said the US could not accept large numbers of migrants, especially refugees, without putting pressure on public resources, creating security concerns, or making it harder for newcomers to integrate. In June, the administration went further by imposing a full travel ban on citizens from 12 countries: Afghanistan, Chad, Congo, Equatorial Guinea, Eritrea, Haiti, Iran, Libya, Myanmar, Somalia, Sudan and Yemen. By October, the White House announced the lowest refugee admissions cap in US history, setting a limit of just 7,500 refugees for the 2026 fiscal year – mostly to be used for white Afrikaners from South Africa. Trump has amplified debunked conspiracy theories alleging a genocide against white South Africans, though data shows that violent crime is high in the country, with victims across races. At the same time, the Trump administration has cut foreign aid programmes that support refugees living in other countries. The administration has also moved to limit skilled immigration, saying the aim is to protect jobs for US citizens. In September, it sharply increased the fee for H-1B visas – used by US companies to hire foreign workers – raising the cost to $100,000 per application. Following the arrest of an Afghan national linked to the [November shooting](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2025/11/27/national-guardsmen-shot-in-washington-dc-what-happened-whos-the-suspect) of two National Guard members in Washington, DC, the government introduced additional travel restrictions. [The ban list was expanded](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2025/12/16/trump-expands-us-travel-ban-to-include-syria-palestine) to include six more countries, beyond the 12 countries whose citizens were previously banned. The six new additions were Palestine, Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger, South Sudan and Syria. Immigration officials also paused asylum cases and stopped processing citizenship and green card applications for people from the countries first affected by the bans. ## Has the Trump administration also been deporting people at record rates? It has. Advertisement By early December, Trump’s Department of Homeland Security said it had deported more than 605,000 people, while another 1.9 million people had “self-deported”. As a result, the US had net negative immigration – more immigrants left the country than those who entered – in 2025, the first time in 50 years that this has happened, according to an analysis by the Brookings Institution. The researchers at Brookings estimated that the net loss of immigrants last year was between 10,000 and 295,000 people. *** Advertisement title: DEPORTATION ON THE INCREASE
description: # Deportations, ICE street arrests are way up — and so are arrests of immigrants with no criminal convictions The jump in arrests and transfers to ICE custody resulted in a sevenfold increase in arrests of people with no convictions, the analysis found. ![A man is detained by a Border Patrol agent on Jan 21, 2026 in Minneapolis.](https://media-cldnry.s-nbcnews.com/image/upload/t_fit-560w,f_auto,q_auto:best/rockcms/2026-01/260127-minneapolis-border-patrol-arrest-mn-1525-c21538.jpg "A man is detained by a Border Patrol agent on Jan 21, 2026 in Minneapolis.") A Border Patrol agent detains a man on in Minneapolis on Jan. 21.Stephen Maturen / Getty Images * * * * * Savewith a NBCUniversal Profile * [Add NBC News to Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=nbcnews.com) Jan. 27, 2026, 6:28 PM EST By [Suzanne Gamboa](https://www.nbcnews.com/author/suzanne-gamboa-ncpn10291) Listen to this article with a free account 00:0003:19 1x In the first nine months of the Trump administration, a jump in the number of immigration-related street arrests led to an increase in the number of deportations initiated inside the U.S. —and away from the border — by more than four and a half times, according to a new report. Researchers from the University of California Berkeley found that Immigration and Customs Enforcement transfers of people from criminal custody to ICE custody as well as street arrests — people who were not in jail at the time — quadrupled over that period. Much of that steep increase was attributable to street arrests rising by more than a factor of 11 — according to [the analysis by the Deportation Data Project](https://deportationdata.org/analysis/immigration-enforcement-first-nine-months-trump.html) at UC Berkeley, a group of academics and lawyers that collect, post and analyze government immigration enforcement data. Even though the overall number of people under ICE custody increased, the people they arrested in this nine-month period were less likely to have criminal convictions. This resulted in a sevenfold increase in arrests of people with no convictions, according to the report. “For both transfers and street arrests, the Trump administration’s decision to stop prioritizing arrests based on factors such as criminal convictions (or to prioritize less) resulted in another well-known trend: the huge increase in the number of arrests of noncitizens not convicted of any crime,” the report said. Arrests of people with convictions also went up, about 30%, but not as much as those without convictions. ![](https://media-cldnry.s-nbcnews.com/image/upload/t_focal-760x428,f_auto,q_auto:best/mpx/2704722219/2026_01/1769463556515_now_mtp_clip_minnesota_260126_1920x1080-1obg7l.jpg) * * * * * [Trump administration ‘shifts’ strategy in Minneapolis following Alex Pretti shooting](https://www.nbcnews.com/meet-the-press/video/trump-administration-shifts-strategy-in-minneapolis-following-alex-pretti-shooting-256604741575) 18:16 President Donald Trump, Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and other administration officials have repeatedly said the president’s mass deportation agenda and his administration’s immigration enforcement activities prioritize and target the [“worst of the worst.”](https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/01/20/dhs-recaps-worst-worst-criminal-illegal-aliens-ice-took-enforcement-action-during) NBC News has reached out to the administration about the report’s findings. ### Recommended [![](https://media-cldnry.s-nbcnews.com/image/upload/t_focal-60x60,f_auto,q_auto:best/rockcms/2026-01/260128-amazon-rs-238867.jpg)](https://www.nbcnews.com/business/business-news/amazon-cuts-16000-jobs-artificial-intelligence-rcna256280) ### [Business News](https://www.nbcnews.com/business)[Amazon slashes another 16,000 jobs](https://www.nbcnews.com/business/business-news/amazon-cuts-16000-jobs-artificial-intelligence-rcna256280) Along with more arrests, ICE had more room to hold immigrant detainees: [When arrests at the border fell,](https://www.nbcnews.com/data-graphics/us-immigration-tracker-follow-arrests-detentions-border-crossings-rcna189148) it freed up space to hold more immigrants arrested and detained within the U.S. The administration adopted rules [such as limiting bond ](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/latino/immigrants-detained-denied-bond-ice-self-deportation-rcna237505)and kept more immigrants detained while they fought their immigration cases, according to the report. The administration also roughly tripled detention beds, using an infusion of [increased funding from Congress, ](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/trumps-ice-force-sweeping-america-billions-tax-spending-cuts-bill-are-rcna254942)and few of those arrested were released. In the last six months of the Biden administration, about 16% of releases occurred within 60 days of arrest. That fell to 3%, the report said. Deportations within two months of detention rose from 55% to 69%, largely because of the lower release rate, the report states. Voluntary departures rose by more than 21 times. “The increase in detention space and immigrants’ decisions not to fight their cases from detention help explain why, even as ICE arrested people who would be more likely to win their cases, such as those without any criminal convictions, the deportation rate among arrestees shot up,” the report states. [![](https://media-cldnry.s-nbcnews.com/image/upload/t_focal-60x60,f_auto,q_auto:best/newscms/2014_06/168326/140116-byline-gamboa-sq-_j4a8736.jpg)](https://www.nbcnews.com/author/suzanne-gamboa-ncpn10291) [Suzanne Gamboa](https://www.nbcnews.com/author/suzanne-gamboa-ncpn10291) Suzanne Gamboa is a national reporter for NBC News.

title: BAN ON 75 COUNTRIES IMMIGRATION UPDATE .
description: # *Trump Administration Sued Over Ban on Immigration From 75 Countries* The Trump administration says these immigrants take welfare intended for Americans, which the lawsuit says is an “unsupported and demonstrably false claim.” Listen to this article · 5:16 min [Learn more](https://help.nytimes.com/hc/en-us/articles/24318293692180) * Share full article * * ![A man in a blue suit walks through a hall with aides.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/02/02/multimedia/02met-sdny-immigration2-phkv/02met-sdny-immigration2-phkv-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&disable=upscale "A man in a blue suit walks through a hall with aides.") Secretary of State Marco Rubio at the Capitol in Washington last month.Credit...Kenny Holston/The New York Times [![Jonah E. Bromwich](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2018/02/16/multimedia/author-jonah-engel-bromwich/author-jonah-engel-bromwich-thumbLarge-v2.png "Jonah E. Bromwich")](https://www.nytimes.com/by/jonah-e-bromwich) By [Jonah E. Bromwich](https://www.nytimes.com/by/jonah-e-bromwich) Feb. 2, 2026Updated 12:01 p.m. ET A group of American citizens, immigration nonprofits and legal organizations on Monday sued Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the State Department, asking a judge [to block a visa ban](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/01/14/us/politics/trump-suspends-visa-75-countries.html) that they said attempted to “eviscerate decades of settled immigration law.” The suit, filed in Manhattan federal court, is the first major attempt to stop the State Department policy announced and implemented last month that suspended the approval of visas for people from 75 countries. More than 85 percent of the countries are non-European and have significant nonwhite populations. The State Department [said in a social media post](https://x.com/StateDept/status/2011478657680757214) last month that the policy, which it has characterized as a pause, was necessary to prevent migration of those who “take welfare from the American people at unacceptable rates.” It added that immigrants from the countries in question “often become public charges,” meaning that they become reliant on the government for subsistence. Advertisement [SKIP ADVERTISEMENT](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/02/nyregion/immigration-ban-lawsuit-75-countries.html#after-story-ad-1) The lawsuit filed on Monday by the National Immigration Law Center and five other legal organizations, calls that an “unsupported and demonstrably false claim,” noting that most people who apply for immigrant visas are not eligible for cash welfare for years. Joanna Cuevas Ingram, a senior staff attorney at the law center, said that the regions and countries from which immigration was banned under the new policy bore an eerie resemblance to quotas enforced by 1920 statutes that were abolished during the civil rights era. She said that her concern was that the justifications in the executive order were a pretext “to limit legal immigration under the actual statute passed by Congress, and to reinstate those old racial quotas.” The State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The State Department policy, which was announced on Jan. 14 and went into effect the following week, is the latest in a string of policies stretching back to the first Trump administration in which President Trump has sought to restrict immigration from countries that he and other top officials have cast as undesirable. Advertisement [SKIP ADVERTISEMENT](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/02/nyregion/immigration-ban-lawsuit-75-countries.html#after-story-ad-2) [In 2018, the Supreme Court upheld his ban on travel](https://www.nytimes.com/2018/06/26/us/politics/supreme-court-trump-travel-ban.html) from several predominantly Muslim countries, saying that as president, Mr. Trump had the authority to secure the country’s borders. The ban implemented last month makes a different argument. [The State Department said](https://travel.state.gov/content/travel/en/News/visas-news/immigrant-visa-processing-updates-for-nationalities-at-high-risk-of-public-benefits-usage.html) it was meant to ensure that immigrants from “high-risk countries do not utilize welfare in the United States.” Experts have said that the policy would [block close to half of all legal immigration.](https://www.washingtonpost.com/immigration/2026/01/21/immigration-visas-75-countries-paused/) ## [Trump Administration: Live Updates](https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/02/02/us/trump-news) Updated Feb. 2, 2026, 9:52 a.m. ET3 hours ago * [Here’s what to know about the partial government shutdown.](https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/02/02/us/trump-news#government-shutdown-what-to-know) * [Here’s what to know about the Kennedy Center.](https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/02/02/us/trump-news#kennedy-center-trump-construction) * [Trump assails the Grammys and threatens to sue Trevor Noah over an Epstein joke.](https://www.nytimes.com/live/2026/02/02/us/trump-news#trump-grammys-trevor-noah) The lawsuit on Monday demonstrates the way that the new ban has already begun to separate families. One of the plaintiffs is a Long Island man and American citizen who has been separated from his young daughter and wife. The man, Cesar Andred Aguirre, returned to Guatemala with his wife, Dania Mariela Escobar, for her visa interview, where the family was informed that Ms. Escobar could not return. Their younger daughter is still nursing and remains in Guatemala with her mother even though she has a disease, Turner syndrome, requiring medical care that is not available there. Advertisement [SKIP ADVERTISEMENT](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/02/nyregion/immigration-ban-lawsuit-75-countries.html#after-story-ad-3) Another plaintiff is a Rochester man and American citizen, Munthaz Mahmud Hassen, who has been separated from his two adolescent children, whose visa petitions and fees were approved and paid but who cannot travel to the United States. And a third, Fernando Lizcano Losada, is a renowned Colombian doctor and endocrinologist who had expected to continue his research at Harvard Medical School. In an interview, Mr. Losada said that with the resources available to him in the United States, he had expected to contribute to meaningful advances in the understanding and treatment of several cancers, including breast cancer. The suit asks a judge to find that the ban is unlawful and to set it aside. It argues, “Congress has never authorized categorical bans, wealth tests or nationality-based presumptions regarding public charge risk.” As the suit notes, in 2019, the Homeland Security Department tried to change its definition of “public charge” to encompass benefits like food stamps, housing vouchers and Medicaid. The administration was sued, and five separate federal courts blocked the implementation of the rule. Advertisement [SKIP ADVERTISEMENT](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/02/nyregion/immigration-ban-lawsuit-75-countries.html#after-story-ad-4) But in Mr. Trump’s second term, his administration has taken advantage of the lag time between the challenge to a given rule and a judge’s finding it to be unlawful to implement its policy choices, regardless of whether they are expected to stand up to judicial scrutiny. Along with the blanket ban on visas, the administration has restored an extensive definition of “public charge,” which the lawsuit is also challenging. Ms. Cuevas Ingram said that the administration was flagrantly violating the law and relying on the likelihood that the resultant litigation would be arduous and time-consuming. She said that it would leave “families and working people who’ve gone through the process and followed all the laws in limbo in a way that is patently discriminatory and insulting to their dignity." [Jonah E. Bromwich](https://www.nytimes.com/by/jonah-e-bromwich) covers criminal justice in the New York region for The Times. title: You May Be Deported
description: # Georgia army veteran deported to Jamaica after routine traffic stop speaks out on ICE detention, systemic failures [![atlanta](https://www-cbsnews-com.cdn.ampproject.org/ii/AW/s/www.cbsnews.com/assets/show/atlanta/logo-square-32.svg "atlanta")](https://www.cbsnews.com/atlanta/?ftag=CNM-00-10aab4i) By [Sharon Lawson](https://www.cbsnews.com/team/sharon-lawson/?ftag=CNM-00-10aab4i), Faysal Aalen Updated on: February 10, 2026 / 11:16 PM EST / CBS Atlanta A [Georgia Army veteran](https://www.cbsnews.com/atlanta/news/georgia-veteran-to-be-deported/?ftag=CNM-00-10aab4i) who spent nearly five decades in the United States was deported to Jamaica following a routine traffic stop, and now he's sharing his story in hopes of sparking change for others in similar situations. [Godfrey Wade,](https://www.cbsnews.com/atlanta/news/georgia-army-veteran-godfrey-wade-deported-jamaica-ice-custody-appeal/?ftag=CNM-00-10aab4i) a legal U.S. resident and Army veteran who first came to America in 1975, was detained after being pulled over for failing to use a turn signal and not carrying his driver's license. What should have been a minor infraction quickly escalated, landing Wade in the custody of [Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)](https://www.cbsnews.com/tag/us-immigration-and-customs-enforcement/?ftag=CNM-00-10aab4i) and ultimately leading to his deportation — despite his honorable military service and long-standing ties to the U.S. Speaking to CBS Atlanta over Zoom from Jamaica, Wade recounted the moment that changed everything: "On that particular Saturday morning, I didn't have a license on me, so I knew just upon being stopped, it's gonna be the officer's discretion whether he releases me with just a fine or he'll take me into jail." Instead of a routine citation, Wade was taken into custody and soon discovered he would not be allowed to post bond. "When you try to bond out, typically you pay a small fee of like $150 and you bond out," he explained. "But ICE has now put a hold on the individual. So now it's up to the discretion of those ICE officers moving forward." Wade was moved from a temporary detainment facility in Lumpkin County to a holding facility in Monroe, Louisiana. There, he waited in what he describes as a "holding zone pending air flight," as ICE filled seats on a monthly charter deportation flight to Jamaica. "Once they get a full manifest, you are kept in Louisiana and they have a scheduling where the Airbus to Jamaica was the first week of each month," Wade said. Wade and his family say his case never appeared before an immigration judge because the original court order was sent to the wrong address — a bureaucratic error that left him with no chance to plead his case. Now back in Jamaica, Wade is speaking out not just for himself, but for the countless others facing deportation without due process. "It's not about Godfrey Wade, it's really about the next veteran, and the next person who really doesn't have the opportunity to articulate that, hey, I need a fair hearing from the constitutional justice system of America." Wade hopes his experience will bring attention to the vulnerabilities faced by veterans and legal residents caught in the immigration system. "There are thousands of people behind me who may be going through a similar situation," he said, calling for reforms to ensure due process and fair hearings for all. ICE has not responded to our request for comment on Wade's deportation.

title: Career & Financial Tips for Immigrants
description: 1. Open a Bank Account Early One of the first things financial advisers suggest when you arrive in a new country is to open a local bank account. It helps you receive paychecks, save money safely, and avoid expensive alternative financial services like check-cashing stores. 2. Build a Real Budget Create a detailed monthly budget that shows: What you earn What you must spend (rent, food, transport) What you can save This makes it easier to plan and avoid surprises — even small savings add up. 3. Start an Emergency Fund Financial experts strongly recommend setting aside money just for emergencies (like medical bills, jobs loss, or car repairs). Even if it’s a small amount each month, an emergency fund provides peace of mind and financial stability. 4. Learn the Credit System Understanding how credit works (credit scores, card use, loan repayment) is critical in many countries. Using credit responsibly helps you build a good financial reputation, which can give you access to better jobs, housing, and loans later. 5. Educate Yourself About Taxes Taxes vary greatly between countries. Learning how taxes work where you live — including filing deadlines and possible deductions or credits — helps you stay compliant and may even reduce the amount you owe. 6. Use Cost-Effective Money Transfers If you send money back home, choosing transparent services with low fees and fair exchange rates like Wise or Remitly can keep more of your money in your hands or your family’s.

title: Hi, My Name is Zara, an aspiring immigrant
description: I admire the courage it takes to leave everything familiar and start over somewhere completely new. Walking away from your support system, the comfort of home, the ease of just existing in a culture you understand - and choosing to rebuild from scratch where even simple things feel hard at first. That takes real faith in yourself. You're constantly adapting, figuring things out, missing home, and still showing up every day to build a life. Hats off to every brave immigrant out there.

title: What was your first week in a new country really like?
description: That first week probably hit you harder than you expected, didn't it? You'd prepared for the big stuff, but nobody tells you how draining it is when even the smallest daily task requires your full attention and courage. The loneliness can feel crushing some days. But I see you - celebrating the small wins like opening a bank account or making it home without getting lost, then sitting alone in your temporary place wondering if you made a mistake. Both of those feelings are completely valid, and it's okay to feel them at the same time. You're doing something incredibly brave, even on the days it doesn't feel like it. I promise it gets easier. You're going to be okay. I hope you find strength in this post. This community is here to help out.

title: What stereotype about immigrants frustrates you the most?
description: For me, it's the assumption that my country of origin must be poor or uninhabitable. It even gets worse when they see my black "African" skin. Like the only reason anyone would ever leave is that they're fleeing disaster or desperate for basic survival. It completely overlooks the fact that people move for ambition, for love, for adventure, for opportunities that fit their specific dreams, not because home was broken. It reduces an entire country, with all its richness and complexity, to a single story of lack. As if good lives, successful careers, and beautiful memories can't exist there. As if choosing to build something new somewhere else means the place you came from had nothing to offer. You can leave a place you love. You can want more without your home being less. Both things can be true. The truth is, moving countries is one of the hardest things you can choose to do. You're starting from zero in a place where nothing comes easy, where you have to prove yourself twice as hard, where homesickness hits you at random moments. There's nothing desperate about that - that's courage. It's absolutely annoying! #rant

title: What was your first week in a new country really like?
description: My first week in the US was honestly a blur of emotions. I remember landing at the airport with two heavy suitcases and feeling both terrified and excited at the same time. The jet lag was brutal, I'd wake up at 3am wide awake and fall asleep at 5pm. Everything felt overwhelming: setting up a bank account, figuring out which SIM card to buy, and even just buying groceries because nothing looked familiar. I stood in the cereal aisle for 10 minutes just staring because I didn't recognize any brands! But I also remember the kindness of a stranger who helped me figure out the subway system when I was completely lost. That small gesture gave me hope that maybe I could figure this out after all.

title: What is one skill you developed because you had to start over?
description: Before immigrating, I was pretty shy about asking for help. I liked figuring things out on my own. But starting over in a new country forced me to become brave enough to ask questions constantly. I had to ask strangers for directions, ask coworkers to explain cultural references I didn't understand, ask my landlord how to work the weird heating system, and ask the pharmacist which medicine was which. Now? I can walk up to anyone and say 'Hi, I'm new here, can you help me?' without feeling embarrassed. Immigration taught me that asking for help isn't weakness,it's how you survive and eventually thrive. It's actually made me more confident, not less.

title: What is one invisible challenge immigrants face?
description: One invisible challenge I don't think people talk about enough is the mental math you're constantly doing; converting currency in your head, translating thoughts before speaking, calculating time zones before calling family, measuring your accent against native speakers, wondering if someone's reaction to you is because of something you did or because of where you're from. It's exhausting in a way that's hard to explain. Not the big dramatic moments, those you prepare for. It's the thousands of tiny micro-decisions and adjustments you make every single day without even realizing it. By 8pm, your brain is just done. Someone asked me once why I seem 'tired all the time' and I couldn't find the words to explain that I'm not physically tired, I'm culturally and linguistically drained. You're not just living your life. You're navigating two worlds at once, code-switching constantly, carrying the weight of representing your country without meaning to, and trying to figure out unwritten rules everyone else seems to know instinctively. And you do it all with a smile because nobody wants to hear the immigrant complain about the opportunity they asked for. That invisible load? It's heavy. And I wish more people understood that.

title: A BIG CHANGE IN US PASSPORT APPLICATIONS.
description: News Article # US State Department Orders Change to Passport Applications *** Published Feb 15, 2026 at 09:55 AM EST updated Feb 15, 2026 at 09:56 AM EST Continue 0:19 / 1:03 ### By Amanda Greenwood Associate News Editor [Newsweek is a Trust Project member](https://www.newsweek.com/editorial-guidelines) The [U.S. State Department](https://www.newsweek.com/topic/u-s-state-department) has ordered certain nonprofit public [libraries](https://www.newsweek.com/topic/libraries) to stop processing passport applications, ending a long-running service that librarians say has operated smoothly and served local needs for years, according to reporting by The Associated Press (AP). ![](https://assets.newsweek.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Copy-of-32-image-2026-02-15T143339.368.png?w=1600&quality=80&webp=1) A sign telling that people they can apply for a U.S. passport, at a post office ...Read More | *Photo by Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images* ## Why the State Department Ordered the Change According to the AP, the agency began issuing cease-and-desist letters to not-for-profit libraries last year, informing them they were no longer authorized to participate in the Passport Acceptance Facility program. A State Department spokesperson said federal law and regulations “[clearly prohibit non‑governmental organizations](https://apnews.com/article/passport-libraries-rubio-nonprofit-0a800e2661c1a07c6a81a40f3801af2f)” from collecting passport application fees, but did not explain why the issue has surfaced now or specify how many libraries were affected. The agency estimated that the number of nonprofit libraries now deemed ineligible to continue with its passport services accounted for less than 1 percent of the total Passport Acceptance Facility program. Data from the American Library Association shows that there are about [1,400 nonprofit libraries in the U.S](https://apnews.com/article/passport-libraries-rubio-nonprofit-0a800e2661c1a07c6a81a40f3801af2f). that could be affected by this change, depending on whether or not they offer passport services. This accounts for about 15 percent of all libraries open to the public. The agency spokesman confirmed that government-run libraries would not be impacted by this change. The AP reported that nonprofit libraries are most common in several Northeastern states. Data from the American Library Association show that they make up about 85 percent of public libraries in Pennsylvania, 56 percent in Maine, 54 percent in Rhode Island, 47 percent in New York, and 46 percent in Connecticut. Read More #### News [Foreign National Parks Visits Tumbling After Trump Changes—Travel Companies](https://www.newsweek.com/foreign-national-parks-visits-tumbling-trump-changes-travel-11528065) [![Dense Fog Sparks Warning For Drivers: ‘Hazardous’](https://assets.newsweek.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/GettyImages-451922923.jpg?w=1600&quality=80&webp=1 "Dense Fog Sparks Warning For Drivers: ‘Hazardous’")](https://www.newsweek.com/dense-fog-sparks-warning-for-drivers-hazardous-11529672) [Dense Fog Sparks Warning For Drivers: ‘Hazardous’](https://www.newsweek.com/dense-fog-sparks-warning-for-drivers-hazardous-11529672) [![Map Shows How Much You Need To Be Rich in Each State](https://assets.newsweek.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Screenshot-2026-02-16-at-13.39.58.png?w=1600&quality=80&webp=1 "Map Shows How Much You Need To Be Rich in Each State")](https://www.newsweek.com/map-how-much-rich-each-state-11528144) [Map Shows How Much You Need To Be Rich in Each State](https://www.newsweek.com/map-how-much-rich-each-state-11528144) [More Related Stories](https://www.newsweek.com/news) ## What Does This Change Mean for the Public? This change is likely to affect libraries that have become key local access points for in‑person passport applications, a role that has helped working families, rural residents, and people with language barriers. “In a time when demand for passports is surging, libraries are among the most accessible passport acceptance facilities, particularly for working families and rural residents,” Democratic and Republican members of Congress from Connecticut, Pennsylvania, New York, New Jersey, and Maryland said in a letter to the Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Cathleen Special, executive director of the Otis Library in Norwich, Connecticut, where passport services ended in November after the order was issued, told the AP: “We still get calls daily seeking that service.” The State Department has defended its decision by noting that more than 7,500 passport acceptance facilities remain nationwide and that over 99 percent of the U.S. population lives within 20 miles of a designated processing location, such as a post office, county clerk’s office, or a government‑run library. The United States Postal Service website says that “thousands of post offices accept first-time passport applications for the U.S. Department of State. Most of those locations can also take your passport photo." The State Department’s passport news page promoted special passport acceptance fairs at approved facilities, and, according to the AP, a spokesperson for the State Department said, “Should the removal of an ineligible facility affect passport services, we will work to identify new eligible program partners in the impacted area.” Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to help produce this story. title: A new episode of Arriving by Immigrant KnowHow is now live on Spotify and Apple Podcasts.
description: **Two Goodbyes, One New Beginning: Maria’s Story of Starting Over** In this deeply moving conversation, Maria Concepcion Nava Guedez shares what it truly means to leave everything behind for the safety and future of your family. Raised in Maracaibo, Venezuela, Maria’s life revolved around her children, her work, and daily visits with her mother and grandmother. When political instability and severe shortages began closing doors around her, she faced an impossible choice: stay and risk her children’s future, or leave and rebuild from nothing. Maria opens up about the fear before her departure, the emotional weight of saying goodbye twice at two airports, and the loneliness of landing in a place where no one knows your name. She speaks candidly about navigating legal systems, enrolling her children in school, and starting over without a support network. Today, she lives with gratitude for the safety and peace she’s found, while still carrying the scent of Lake Maracaibo and the blazing sun of her hometown in her heart. Her story is about resilience, identity, and what it means to love two countries at once. This episode is for anyone who has ever had to begin again, and for those who want to understand what that truly costs. Listen now on [Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/show/55YursJ24oxF1QFwdCOVj0?si=3902e3cb4ff7491f) and [Apple Podcasts.](https://podcasts.apple.com/ph/podcast/arriving-by-immigrant-knowhow/id1838365608)

title: Growing Up With An Immigrant Family
description: Growing up with Pakistani parents meant learning how to balance two worlds at once. I had to carry my family's values and language while also learning to grow with my peers. I had to create a third culture to follow from a very young age. It meant that the food I brought to school was not the typical Lunchables, but rather roti and chutneys to eat with it. The kids I grew up with didn't understand that, but I still preferred homemade meals over processed foods like Lunchables. It also meant that, when my parents wanted me to observe the same traditions they upheld when they were growing up, I chose what was best for me instead. Developing this third culture was not always easy, but as an adult now, I am really glad I was able to persevere and reap the benefits of both cultures I grew up in. This experience shaped me into someone adaptable, resilient, and deeply appreciative of diversity. It taught me the importance of embracing both my heritage and the opportunities that come with living between cultures.

title: NEW PASSPORT RULES FOR BRITISH-CANADIAN DUAL CITIZENS
description: *Starting Feb. 25, British dual nationals must present a British or Irish passport, a certificate of entitlement or an emergency travel document in order to enter the U.K.* Author of the article: By Adrianna Teal, [National Post](https://nationalpost.com/author/natpost/) Published Feb 24, 2026 Last updated 4 hours ago 3 minute read [21 Comments](https://nationalpost.com/news/canada/new-passport-rules-for-british-canadian-dual-citizens#comments-area) ![British pasport.](https://smartcdn.gprod.postmedia.digital/nationalpost/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/British-passport-1.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=288&h=216&sig=9qPqfFKC8w9pp5tvqeuiEA "British pasport.") From Feb. 25, British dual nationals must present a British or Irish passport, a certificate of entitlement tied to a foreign passport, or an emergency travel document in order to enter the country. Photo by ANTHONY WALLACE/AFP via Getty Images Article content Dual British-Canadian citizens who have long been able to travel to the United Kingdom on a Canadian passport alone will soon need to rethink their travel routine. Starting Wednesday, the U.K. will require dual nationals to show official proof of their British status before they can enter the country. Article content ### What’s changing? Article content Article content From Feb. 25, British dual nationals must present a British or Irish passport, a certificate of entitlement tied to a foreign passport, or an emergency travel document in order to enter the country. A Canadian passport alone will no longer be enough to claim entry as a citizen, even for those who have held British nationality their entire lives. Article content Advertisement 1 Story continues below Article content According to the U.K. government website, citizenship can be verified with either a British or Irish passport, an emergency travel document, or any other valid passport with a certificate of entitlement. Article content ![Posted](https://dcs-static.gprod.postmedia.digital/20.6.2/websites/images/newsletters/icon-np-posted.svg "Posted") NP Posted Get a dash of perspective along with the trending news of the day in a very readable format. Sign Up By signing up you consent to receive the above newsletter from Postmedia Network Inc. Interested in more newsletters? [Browse here.](https://nationalpost.com/newsletters) Article content ### Why is it changing? Article content The new requirement is part of the U.K.’s rollout of its Electronic Travel Authorization (ETA) system, designed to strengthen border security by pre-screening visa-exempt visitors with biometric, biographic, and criminality checks before they board flights, allowing authorities to block high-risk individuals remotely. Article content Applying for ETA will run visitors around $30 and enables visits for the next two years. Article content British and Irish citizens cannot apply for ETA and will be denied if they do so. Article content ### How does it impact British Canadians? Article content For many dual citizens, routine trips to visit family or friends will now effectively require two passports: a Canadian one to meet rules for returning home and a British passport — or equivalent documentation — to enter the U.K. Article content Older emigrants or people who left the country as children may face difficulties if they have not kept their paperwork current, while occasional travellers could be caught off guard during the transition. Article content Advertisement 2 Story continues below Article content Read More 1. [![A Canadian passport is shown in this image.](https://smartcdn.gprod.postmedia.digital/nationalpost/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/1207-br-library.BR_-scaled.jpg?h=96&strip=all&quality=5&sig=ul2UH7Xw7KDXgA1IT9IWoQ "A Canadian passport is shown in this image.")](https://nationalpost.com/news/canada/uk-travel-policy-enforce-canadians) [Canadians will need 'advance permission' to travel to U.K. starting in 2026](https://nationalpost.com/news/canada/uk-travel-policy-enforce-canadians) 2. [![A person uses the Automated European Union Entry/Exit System (EES) kiosk during a press preview on the rollout of the system at Eurotunnel, England, on Sept. 23, 2025.](https://smartcdn.gprod.postmedia.digital/nationalpost/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/GettyImages-2236679809-1.jpg?h=96&strip=all&quality=5&sig=WvMjaF-zpwQlBEiNxxLKkw "A person uses the Automated European Union Entry/Exit System (EES) kiosk during a press preview on the rollout of the system at Eurotunnel, England, on Sept. 23, 2025.")](https://nationalpost.com/news/europe-entry-exit-system-canadian) [Canadians travelling to Europe face new visa requirements](https://nationalpost.com/news/europe-entry-exit-system-canadian) 3. Advertisement 1 Article content ### How much does it cost to renew or create a British passport? Article content Dual citizens can apply for a British passport online, costing approximately $185 for the application, plus shipping costs. Processing can take several weeks and may take longer for first-time applications who need to provide additional documentation. Article content ### What if you don’t have a British passport? Article content Without a British passport, dual citizens have a few options. Article content Applying for a British passport remains the most straightforward route. Those who qualify but prefer not to hold one, or need to travel sooner, can apply for a certificate of entitlement, which confirms the right to live and work in the U.K. while linked to a foreign passport. Article content Applications are typically processed within 3 weeks and allow travellers to keep their existing passport during processing Article content However, at roughly $1,100, a certificate of entitlement is significantly more expensive than a passport and must be reapplied for when a new foreign passport is issued, making it less practical for frequent travellers. Article content Travelling solely as a Canadian visitor is not considered a reliable workaround, as British citizens are expected to demonstrate their status and may be refused board if they cannot. Article content Airlines may make exceptions for expired passports, but are not required to do so. Article content ### What the changes don’t do Article content The new rules do not affect citizenship itself. Dual nationals still retain the right to live and work in the U.K. Article content *Our website is the place for the latest breaking news, exclusive scoops, longreads and provocative commentary. title: GREEN CARD UPDATE
description: News Article # Green Card Update: New Visa Fees Come Into Effect—Full List of Changes *** Published Mar 03, 2026 at 09:17 AM EST updated Mar 03, 2026 at 09:18 AM EST Continue ### By Sam Stevenson Associate News Editor [Newsweek is a Trust Project member](https://www.newsweek.com/editorial-guidelines) U.S. immigration officials have raised fees for fast‑tracked visa and green card applications, adding new costs for workers and employers seeking quicker decisions. ## Why It Matters The fee change follows a federal rule allowing regular inflation‑based adjustments to [immigration](https://www.newsweek.com/topic/immigration) services, and it comes as demand for faster processing remains high [amid long backlogs](https://www.newsweek.com/green-card-change-tremendous-effect-backlog-ex-official-warns-11149210). ![Hand touching envelope from USCIS on flag of USA background - stock photo](https://assets.newsweek.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/Copy-of-32-Split-Screen-2026-03-03T131541.784.png?w=1600&quality=80&webp=1 "Hand touching envelope from USCIS on flag of USA background - stock photo") A stock photo showing a letter from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services an...Read More | *Getty Images* ## What To Know New premium processing fees from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services ([USCIS](https://www.newsweek.com/topic/uscis)) took effect on March 1, applying to requests postmarked on or after that date. USCIS raised premium processing fees by different amounts depending on the type of visa or green card petition, with most employment visas and employment‑based green cards now costing $2,965 for faster processing. The increase affects applicants who pay extra to have certain immigration cases handled more quickly. Premium processing is an optional service that allows USCIS to commit to a fixed review timeline, usually between 15 and 45 days, [depending on the application type](https://www.newsweek.com/green-card-update-changes-applicants-11358580). It does not guarantee approval, only faster action. Requests are made using Form I‑907. For employment‑based green cards, the key change applies to Form I‑140, which covers petitions for foreign workers seeking permanent residence through their job. The premium processing fee for I‑140 petitions increased from $2,805 to $2,965. This confirms that the change is tied specifically to employment‑based filings, not family‑based green cards. The same $2,965 fee now applies to many [employment visa petitions](https://www.newsweek.com/green-card-update-applicants-for-2027-receive-boost-11418395) filed on Form I‑129, including H‑1B and L‑1 visas. Lower‑tier increases affect some religious and seasonal worker visas, while separate hikes apply to student work authorization and change‑of‑status applications. USCIS has warned that applications sent with outdated fees will be rejected, potentially causing delays for people relying on quick decisions to start or continue work in the United States. The agency said the added revenue would be used to support premium processing services and reduce case backlogs. ## Full List of Changes USCIS has introduced tiered increases to premium processing fees based on the type of application, according to the rule. For H‑2B seasonal workers and R‑1 religious workers filing Form I‑129, the premium processing fee increased from $1,685 to $1,780. For all other eligible Form I‑129 work visas—including H‑1B, L‑1, O‑1, P, Q, E and TN classifications—the fee rose from $2,805 to $2,965. Employment‑based green card petitions filed on Form I‑140, including EB‑1, EB‑2 (with and without a National Interest Waiver), and EB‑3 categories, are also now subject to the $2,965 premium processing fee. Premium processing fees for certain change‑of‑status or extension applications filed on Form I‑539—including F, J and M nonimmigrant categories and qualifying dependents—increased from $1,965 to $2,075. For employment authorization applications filed on Form I‑765, including eligible OPT and STEM‑OPT cases, the premium processing fee increased from $1,685 to $1,780. ## What People Are Saying **The U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services said on its website: **"This rule is effective March 1, 2026. If you submit a request for premium processing postmarked on or after March 1, 2026, you must include the new fee for the specific benefit you are requesting.
